title: Sustainable recycling of polyester wastes using a coordinatively unsaturated Zn catalyst

paper_content.abstract:
Closed-loop recycling of polyester waste offers a promising route for addressing the environmental burden of plastic pollution and enabling resource circularity. However, current polyester plastic recycling methods face limitations in industrial scalability and environmental impact. Here, we report the development of a low-cost, earth-abundant, coordinatively unsaturated defect–zinc oxide (d–ZnO) catalyst for the efficient depolymerization of various polyester wastes, including polyethylene terephthalate, biodegradable polyesters, post-consumer polyesters, and mixed polyester waste.

Mechanistic investigations reveal that defects structure in the catalyst enhance the activation of oxygen and water molecules, generating nucleophilic species that drive ester bond cleavage via carbonyl activation. The robustness and scalability of our strategy were further validated through large-scale closed-loop recycling of polyester waste plastics. Life cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analysis (TEA) demonstrate the environmental sustainability and economic viability of this process across multiple metrics, including human health, ecosystem quality, resource consumption, and production cost. This work offers a broadly applicable, sustainable, and practical solution for management polyester plastic waste.
paper_content.introduction:
Polyesters are synthetic polymers featuring ester linkages and are produced at a scale exceeding 70 million tons per year for use in packaging, bottles, and textiles1, 2. The widespread accumulation of polyester plastic waste has had profound impacts on the environment, marine ecosystems, and human health3–5. Chemical depolymerization of polyesters into monomeric constituents via hydrolysis6–9, alcoholysis10–16, aminolysis17, 18 and hydrogenolysis19–21 has been widely investigated. These processes offer a viable and scalable alternative to conventional end-of-life treatments, including mechanical recycling, incineration and landfilling22–25. However, pyrolysis and hydrogenolysis typically yield complex mixtures with low product selectivity. In contrast, solvent-assisted depolymerization of polyesters enables controlled cleavage of ester bonds to selectively yield targeted monomers. For instance, polyethylene terephthalate (PET) waste can be hydrolyzed in neutral aqueous media to produce terephthalic acid (TPA), which is suitable for repolymerization into recycled PET.

Nevertheless, conventional hydrolysis of polyesters typically requires harsh conditions, including strongly acidic or basic media or high-pressure systems (Figure 1a), leading to reactor corrosion, complex wastewater treatment, and elevated energy demands26, 27. Recent emerging strategies (including in situ alkaline hydrolysis, solvent-assisted hydrolysis, binuclear Zn-catalyzed hydrolysis, and acetic acid-mediated depolymerization) have improved PET conversion efficiency (Figure 1b)28–32. However, these methods often involve alkaline environments that necessitate post-neutralization and the use of mixed solvents, which complicate product separation and increase process energy intensity. Therefore, there remains a critical need for catalytic systems that enable selective polyester depolymerization under neutral, organic solvent-free conditions.

Homogeneous catalysts, such as ionic liquids and metal salts have demonstrated high activity in polyester depolymerization33–35. Recently, metal-based heterogeneous catalysts supported by auxiliary ligands have also been reported. For example, Dove and co-workers developed a highly stable bimetallic “acid salt” catalyst system capable of depolymerizing PET and polylactic acid (PLA), achieving activities up to 1.32×105 g mol –1 h–1 at 180 °C 36. In addition, Wang et al. reported a tetranuclear titanium catalyst that exhibits exceptionally high activity for PET methanolysis, reaching 1.9 ×107 g mol –1 h–1 at a catalyst loading of only 0.005 mol% 37. However, ionic liquids require tedious purification, and residual metal ions from metal salts catalysts can hinder repolymerization. In contrast, heterogeneous catalysts offer superior stability and ease of separation, making them attractive for polyester recycling.

Nevertheless, several key challenges persist: (I) limited interfacial contact due to poor multiphase mass transfer among solid polyester, water, and catalyst. (II) Polyester hydrolysis relies on activation of water molecules by catalytic sites to facilitate ester bond cleavage, underscoring the importance of enhancing the affinity and activation of water on catalyst surfaces. (III) Conventional approaches to improve heterogeneous catalyst activity focus on modifying particle size, coupling with ionic liquids, or employing porous materials. These mainly tune surface-active sites or increase external surface area, but can compromise catalyst–substrate mass transfer efficiency and reduce overall reactivity. To address these limitations, innovative catalyst designs and deeper mechanistic insights are essential for enabling efficient and green chemical recycling of PET waste.

In this work, we development of coordinatively unsaturated defect–zinc oxide (d–ZnO) nanosheets as an efficient heterogeneous catalyst for polyester hydrolysis (Figure 1c). Under neutral aqueous conditions at 190 °C, d–ZnO enabled complete depolymerization of PET, affording terephthalic acid (TPA) in >99% selectivity and achieving a space–time yield (STY) an order of magnitude higher than prior reports. The presence of oxygen molecules (O2) was found to be essential for enhancing catalytic activity, while the combination of defects in d–ZnO played a pivotal role in selective C–O bond cleavage. In situ infrared spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that defect sites facilitate the activation of water and O2 to generate nucleophilic species, which selectively attack ester carbonyl groups and promote bond scission. The catalyst demonstrated remarkable tolerance to additives and impurities across a wide range of polyester feedstocks. Moreover, we demonstrate the successful repolymerization of recovered TPA into recycled PET, enabling a closed-loop recycling process. Life cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analysis (TEA) comparisons against glycolysis, methanolysis, hydrolysis, and petroleum-based production systems confirm that this neutral hydrolysis approach offers superior environmental and economic performance. This work presents a viable and scalable approach for advancing circularity in polyester recycling.
paper_content.results:
Characterization of catalysts
To enable catalytic polyester depolymerization, we synthesized coordinatively unsaturated defect–zinc oxide (d–ZnO) nanosheets via an -ascorbic acid-assisted etching strategy. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images demonstrate that the d–ZnO retain the overall morphology and grain size of the pristine ZnO (p–ZnO) nanosheets (Figures 2a, b). Upon addition of -ascorbic acid, the sample color gradually changed from white to light yellow (insets of Figures 2a, b), suggesting structural changes. The strong interaction between -ascorbic and ZnO during the etching process promotes the generation of lattice defects. Although the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of d–ZnO and p–ZnO exhibit similar overall features (Supplementary Figure 1), noticeable changes in the intensity of the (002) and (110) reflections suggest the introduction of a significant number of lattices vacancies38.

Aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-STEM) revealed locally disordered lattice regions within d–ZnO nanosheets, consistent with the presence of unsaturated Zn coordination sites (Figure 2c)39. Zn K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra show a shift to lower energy for d–ZnO compared to Zn foil and ZnO, indicative of a lower oxidation state of Zn in the defective lattice (Figure 2d)40. Moreover, Fourier-transformed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (FT-EXAFS) analysis confirmed that the local coordination environment around Zn atoms in d–ZnO remains close to that of Zn–O bonding (Figure 2e). Electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy was employed to assess unpaired electrons associated with defect sites (Figure 2f). The signal at g = 2.002 is assigned to electron trapping by oxygen vacancies (Ov), while the signal at g = 1.950 corresponds to electron trapping by zinc vacancies (Znv)39, 41. Compared to p–ZnO, d–ZnO displayed substantially enhanced Ov and Znv signals, corroborating the L-ascorbic acid-induced formation of surface lattice defects.

Catalytic depolymerization of PET and real polyester waste over d–ZnO.
To investigate the catalytic depolymerization of polyester, polyethylene terephthalate (PET; number-average molecular weight (Mn) = 32 kDa, Supplementary Figure 2) was used as the model substrate. PET was reacted with the catalyst and water in a high-temperature and high-pressure reactor at 190 °C for 6 h. After cooling to room temperature, the products were collected and analyzed by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and gel permeation chromatography (GPC) to determine composition and purity.

We found that the reaction atmosphere plays a crucial role in determining product selectivity. Depolymerization reactions were conducted under nitrogen and varying concentrations of O2/N2 atmospheres using PET (Mn =32 kDa) as the substrate. Under a nitrogen atmosphere at 190 °C and neutral pH, p–ZnO exhibited minimal catalytic activity, yielding <5% PET conversion after 6 h. The product distribution included only 0.7% terephthalic acid (TPA), 4.3% oligomers (Figure 3a, Supplementary Figure 4, and Supplementary Table 1). Upon increasing the oxygen concentration from 1% to 10%, a marked decrease in byproduct formation was observed alongside a corresponding improvement in TPA selectivity, indicating the critical role of molecular oxygen in governing product distribution. At a 20%O2/80% N2 or under ambient air, complete PET depolymerization was achieved within 6 h, affording a TPA yield of 99%, and <1% yield of oligomers (Figure 3a, Supplementary Figures 5–12, and Supplementary Table 1). These findings unequivocally demonstrate that molecular oxygen is indispensable for promoting the selective hydrolysis of PET over p–ZnO.

To further optimize the reaction, the effects of temperature, reaction time, and catalyst dosage were systematically investigated (Supplementary Table 2), achieving >99% TPA yield with 99% purity under optimal conditions. The d–ZnO achieved substantially higher PET conversion and TPA selectivity compared to the p–ZnO and commercial ZnO (Figure 3b, Supplementary Figures 13, 14, and Supplementary Table 1), emphasizing the critical role of defect sites functionality in catalytic performance. Moreover, a series of defect–rich metal oxides were synthesized using analogous synthetic protocols. Their catalytic activities exhibited a strong correlation with the intrinsic Lewis acidity of the constituent metal ions, following the trend: d–ZnO > MgO > CaO > Co3O4 > MnO > Fe2O3 > Fe3O4 > Al2O3 >TiO2 > ZrO2 > Nb2O5 > CeO2 > SiO2 (Figure 3c, Supplementary Figures 15–38, and Supplementary Table 3), which closely aligns with the relative Lewis acid strengths of the corresponding divalent metal ions.

Under optimized conditions, PET waste was completely depolymerized over d–ZnO via hydrolysis at 190 °C within 6 h. The process afforded a space-time yield (STY) of 56 g h–1 g cat–1, which is an order of magnitude higher than those reported for conventional hydrolysis catalysts (Figure 3d, Supplementary Table 4). STY was calculated as the mass of product obtained per gram of catalyst per hour. Considering variations in previous reports, hydrolysis conditions were classified into four categories: (1) supercritical CO2, (2) acidic hydrolysis, (3) alkaline hydrolysis, (4) neutral hydrolysis, and (5) hydrogenolysis. Under neutral aqueous conditions (≥190 °C), d–ZnO exhibited significantly higher catalytic activity than previously reported systems. Even in comparison to supercritical CO2 and acidic or basic conditions, d–ZnO outperformed in catalytic efficiency. Notably, while acidic and alkaline systems can enable PET degradation at lower temperatures, they typically operate under harsh pH conditions (pH < 1 or pH > 10), raising environmental and operational concerns.

We further evaluated the depolymerization performance of d–ZnO across a variety of polyester substrates and mixed plastic waste. Structurally analogous polyesters to PET, such as polybutylene terephthalate (PBT) and polytrimethylene terephthalate (PTET), were efficiently depolymerized into terephthalic acid (TPA) with yields exceeding 99%, while poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) has a yield of 86%. (Figure 3e, Supplementary Figures 39–41, and Supplementary Table 5). Polycarbonate (PC) similarly depolymerized to bisphenol A (BPA) with yields >99% (Figure 3e, Supplementary Figure 42, and Supplementary Table 5). Encouraged by these results, we further explored the depolymerization of bio-based polyesters. Polycaprolactone (PCL) was converted into 6-hydroxyhexanoic acid, polylactic acid (PLA) into lactic acid, poly(butylene adipate) (PBA) and poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) into 1,4-butanediol, all with yields above 96% (Figure 3e, Supplementary Figures 43–46, and Supplementary Table 5).

To assess the practical applicability of our catalytic system, we examined the depolymerization of post-consumer PET waste and complex plastic mixtures using d–ZnO. In model systems containing PET and common packaging plastics (PLA, PC, PE, PP, PS, and PVC), selective hydrolysis of PET proceeded efficiently, affording TPA in yields exceeding 98%, with negligible interference from mixed plastics (Figure 3f, Supplementary Table 5). Remarkably, a wide range of real-world PET waste, including transparent and colored bottles was fully depolymerized under identical conditions, affording TPA in yields exceeding 99% (Figure 3f, Supplementary Table 5). These findings indicate that typical additives such as plasticizers, stabilizers, and antioxidants do not compromise catalyst performance. Depolymerization of polyester textiles and blended cotton/fabrics, despite the presence of complex additives like dyes, adhesives, and UV stabilizers, also affording TPA in yields exceeding 98% (Figure 3f, Supplementary Table 5). While dye removal remains a challenge in aqueous systems, nearly complete decolorization was achieved through activated carbon adsorption, although the fate of dye-laden carbon requires further attention. Remarkably, d–ZnO retained high catalytic activity even for complex substrates such as carpets composed of synthetic/natural fiber blends and various additives, affording >90% yield of TPA under ambient air conditions (Figure 3f, Supplementary Table 5).

Importantly, d–ZnO also demonstrated excellent performance in laboratory large-scale depolymerization of PET flakes (40 g), yielding over 34.5 g of high purity (>99%, Supplementary Figure 47) recovered TPA, which was subsequently repolymerized into recycled PET (r-PET). The r-PET was analyzed by ¹H NMR spectroscopy (Supplementary Figure 48), where the emergence of PET backbone signals at δ = 4.8 ppm confirmed the formation of r-PET. GPC revealed that the Mn =26 kDa of r-PET (Supplementary Figure 49), only slightly lower than that of the PET feedstock (Mn =32 kDa). The catalyst displayed excellent stability and recyclability, maintaining high activity and selectivity over five consecutive cycles (Supplementary Figure 50). Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) analysis of the digested TPA product confirmed that no Zn2+ leaching occurred. Following regeneration (see Supplementary Methods), the catalytic performance of d–ZnO was fully restored. XRD and SEM analyses (Supplementary Figure 51) confirmed that the regenerated catalyst retained both the crystalline structure and morphology of the original material. These results collectively underscore the robustness and versatility of the d–ZnO catalyst in addressing diverse streams of polyester waste, offering a promising avenue for closed-loop chemical recycling under mild, scalable conditions.

Mechanistic studies for the depolymerization pathway
To elucidate the evolution of active sites on the catalyst surface in the presence of reactive gas atmospheres and water molecules, semi-in situ electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy was employed to monitor signal variations of d–ZnO under air at various reaction temperatures (Figure 4a). The ESR signals at g = 2.002 and g = 1.950 are assigned to oxygen vacancies (Ov) and zinc vacancies (Znv), respectively, arising from the low-coordination environment induced by defect formation. As the temperature increased under air, the signal intensities of both Ov and Znv gradually increased, indicating that oxygen facilitates defect generation within d–ZnO42, 43. In contrast, under a N2 atmosphere, the Znv signal remained unchanged (Figure 4b), suggesting that defect evolution is suppressed in the absence of oxygen. To further probe the nature of surface-adsorbed oxygen species, low-temperature electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy was conducted at 110 K (Figure 4c). d–ZnO exhibited a pronounced signal at g = 2.001, attributed to surface-bound O3– species, whereas commercial ZnO showed no detectable signal. Upon heating to 150 K, O3– species are known to dissociate into monoatomic O– species, indicating that the active oxygen species stabilized on d–ZnO are predominantly O– species44.

To elucidate the activation mechanism of the solvent (H2O) on the surface of d–ZnO, in situ attenuated total reflectance fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIRS) spectroscopy was performed by gradually increasing the temperature from 25 °C to 190 °C. The v(O–H) stretching signal observed in the 3500–3150 cm–1 region corresponding to hydroxyl groups. A red shift of the v(O–H) stretching mode, along with an enhanced signal near 3150 cm–1, suggests that defect sites on d–ZnO promote interfacial water adsorption and O–H bond activation (Figure 4d)45, 46. We further evaluated the energy barriers associated with O2 and H2O activation on bulk ZnO, d–ZnO with oxygen vacancies (d–ZnO–Ov), and d–ZnO with zinc vacancies (d–ZnO–ZnVC), focusing on the O2 → O2* and H2O + O2* → OOH* + OH* steps (Supplementary Data 1). The local defect structures of d–ZnO act as anchoring sites for both O2 and H2O molecules, forming the initial state (S1). Water molecules adsorbed at S1* are activated by O2 to generate an intermediate species S2*, which further transforms into a transition state (TS), eventually yielding nucleophilic species in the final state. Notably, the activation energy for TS formation on d–ZnO–Znv is as low as 0.055 eV (Figure 4e, Supplementary Figure 52, and Supplementary Table 6), compared to 0.89 eV for d–ZnO–Ov and 1.24 eV for bulk ZnO (Figure 4e, Supplementary Figures 53, 54, and Supplementary Tables 7, 8). These results highlight the superior activity of defect structures on d–ZnO in facilitating both O2 and H2O activation pathways, which is critical for ester bond cleavage in PET depolymerization. This mechanistic insight aligns well with the in situ FTIR observations, emphasizing the essential role of d–ZnO defects in catalytic O2 and H2O activation.

To elucidate the depolymerization mechanism of PET over the catalyst, synchrotron radiation in situ infrared (IR) spectroscopy was employed using a dimer model compound (Mode) to simulate polyester conversion to monomers (Figure 4f, Supplementary Figure 55). The evolution of characteristic vibrational modes during hydrolysis was monitored in real-time to reveal potential intermediates and reaction pathways. At the initial stage, characteristic IR bands for Mode in H2O include the ν(C=O) stretching at 1,727 cm–1, ν(C–O–H) at 1406 cm−1, ν(C–O–C) at 1,338 cm–1, ν(C–O) at 1,259 cm–1, and ν(C–OH) at 1,083 cm–1 47, 48. With the presence of the d–ZnO sites, the ν(C=O) and ν(C–O–H) presented a red shift from 1,727 cm−1 to 1,708 cm−1 and 1,406 cm−1 to 1,390 cm−1, respectively (Figure 4f). This suggests that the carbonyl group produces a bond-weakening effect when coordinated to zinc sites, thereby enhancing the electrophilicity of the Mode31, 49. Notably, the ν(O=C–O) band at 1126 cm⁻¹ gradually disappears, accompanied by the emergence of a ν(C–OH) band at 1083 cm⁻¹, indicating cleavage of O=C–O–CH3 and O=C–O–CH2 ester bonds and the formation of methanol or ethylene glycol. Furthermore, the disappearance of the ν(C–O–C) signal at 1,338 cm–1 suggests cleavage of the C–O–CH3 or C–O–CH2 bond in Mode. These observations indicate that the ester C–O bond in Mode is cleaved, and methanol and ethylene glycol units are released and linked to form TPA. Meanwhile, the terminal groups are capped by hydrogen atoms to yield methanol and ethylene glycol, confirming that C–O bond cleavage within ester groups is the key step during PECT hydrolysis.

Hydrolysis experiments using model compounds (dimethyl terephthalate (DMT), bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET), and Mode-d4) were performed to elucidate ester bond-cleavage pathways. 1H NMR analysis showed that DMT hydrolysis produced terephthalic acid (TPA), with characteristic aromatic (8.13 ppm) and carboxyl (13.4 ppm) signals, while the presence of an O–CH3 signal at 3.89 ppm indicates cleavage at the O=C–O–CH3 bond (Supplementary Figure 56a). BHET hydrolysis similarly yielded TPA, with methylene resonances at 4.32 and 3.72 ppm confirming cleavage at the O=C–O–CH2 linkage. For Mode-d4, both O=C–O–CH3 and O=C–O–CD2 bond cleavage pathways were observed. Infrared spectroscopy further confirmed TPA formation, with benzene ring vibrations at 1574 cm–1 and C=O stretching at 1688 cm–1 (Supplementary Figure 56b). Residual O–CH3 (1192 cm–1) and CH2–OH (1065 cm–1) vibrations indicate partially hydrolyzed intermediates.

To gain further mechanistic insight into the role of catalyst surface defects in polyester depolymerization, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were conducted using Mode as the model substrate (Supplementary Data 1). The activation and cleavage of the ester C–O bond was examined on bulk ZnO, d–ZnO with oxygen vacancies (d–ZnO–Ov), and d–ZnO with zinc vacancies (d–ZnO–Znv). During depolymerization, the adsorption of OOH* and OH* on d–ZnO–Ov surfaces facilitate their interaction with Mode to form the initial state (IS1*, ΔE = –0.94 eV) (Figure 4g, Supplementary Figure 57, and Supplementary Table 9). Synergistic interactions between surface defects and OOH* species promote cleavage of the ester linkage (O=C–O–CH2), resulting in an intermediate state (IS3*, ΔE = 0.18 eV). Further transformation via the transition state TS1 (ΔE = 0.38 eV) drives scission of the C–O bond (O=C–O–CH3), sequentially generating TPA, 1-(2-hydroxyethyl)-4-methyl terephthalate (HEMT), ethylene glycol and methanol. The corresponding activation energies for this step are 0.56 eV on bulk ZnO and 0.52 eV on the d–ZnO–Znv (Figure 4g, Supplementary Figures 58, 59, and Supplementary Tables 10, 11). Similarly, the ester bond in HEMT (O=C–O–CH3) is activated and cleaved in the presence of OOH* and OH*, producing TPA and methanol via TS2 (ΔE = 0.46 eV). The activation energy barriers for C–O bond scission in HEMT is 0.49 eV on bulk ZnO and 0.52 eV on d–ZnO–Znv.

Based on the above findings, a schematic representation of the hydrolysis pathway catalyzed by d–ZnO is illustrated in Supplementary Figure 60. Molecular oxygen and water are first adsorbed and subsequently activated on the surface of d–ZnO, generating reactive OOH* and OH*species. These species nucleophilic attack the carbonyl carbon of PET, while the carbonyl oxygen is simultaneously activated by the d–ZnO of Zn sites. This synergistic effect enhances the cleavage of C–O bonds, leading to the formation of oligomers. Through a series of subsequent steps, comprising O2 and H2O activation, further nucleophilic attacks, carbonyl activation, and C–O bond scission.

LCA and TEA for closed-loop recycling PET
Sustainability assessments are crucial for evaluating the environmental, social, and economic impacts of recycling processes. To assess the environmental impact of the staged polyester recycling process, a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) was conducted using a cutoff approach50. Activity data for the process were obtained by constructing a conceptual factory model using Aspen software (Supplementary Figure 61). The model begins with polyester waste as the input stage and concludes with the recovered recycled polyester (Supplementary Table 12). The conceptual factory’s annual processing capacity is set at 250,000 tons, based on polyester waste statistics. The modeling process for staged polyester waste recycling includes several phases (Supplementary Figure 62, Supplementary Tables 13–15): (1) collection, transportation, and pretreatment of polyester waste; (2) catalyst synthesis, polyester depolymerization, and product separation; (3) repolymerization, and (4) melt extrusion and pelletizing. To improve modeling accuracy, experimental, literature, and industry data were incorporated into the comprehensive simulation of the entire recycling process. Background data on chemicals and electricity production were sourced from the ecoinvent v3.7 database.

Using recycled polyester pellets as the endpoint for assessment, the environmental impact of polyester closed-loop recycling process was compared with that of petroleum-based synthetic processes, including human health, resource consumption, and ecosystem impact9. Notably, the process demonstrated favorable performance in two critical metrics: Global Warming Potential (GWP) and non-renewable energy use (NREU). In China, the GWP is 2.830 kg CO2-eq/kg and the NREU is 40.377 MJ/kg (Figure 5a, Supplementary Table 16), which are approximately 47.3% and 55.1% lower than the petroleum-based production route, respectively. In Europe, the GWP is 2.236 kg CO2-eq/kg and the NREU is 38.125 MJ/kg (Figure 5b, Supplementary Table 16), which are approximately 7.2% and 45.5% lower than the petroleum-based production route, respectively. The key factors contributing to these impacts were the consumption of energy (electricity and steam) and chemicals. The polyester closed-loop recycling process significantly reduced environmental impact, primarily due to its integrated energy application and high recycling efficiency (Figure 5c, Supplementary Tables 17–26). Furthermore, we evaluated the environmental impact of d–ZnO across the full recycling process (Supplementary Figure 63 and Supplementary Tables 27, 28). Terrestrial ecotoxicity and non-carcinogenic human toxicity accounted for approximately 20% and 5% of the total impact, respectively, whereas contributions from other categories were minimal. The d–ZnO catalyst remained structurally stable throughout the reaction, and no Zn2+ leaching was detected, indicating that dissolved zinc species are not introduced into the environment. Additionally, a comparison with methanolysis, hydrolysis, and petroleum-based production processes (Figures 5d, 5e) identified core comparison metrics: global warming potential, and non-renewable energy use. With the exception of wastewater generation, which was similar to the petroleum-based production process, the hydrolysis recycling process outperformed the alternatives in all other metrics.

Through techno-economic analysis, we compared the total capital investment and unit production costs of the staged polyester closed-loop recycling process with those of the petroleum-based synthetic process (Figure 5f, 5g). The minimum selling price (MSP) of TPA was assessed for different production routes based on PET feedstocks (Supplementary Tables 29–35). Using clean PET sources results in a relatively high MSP of $1,049 per ton due to higher feedstock costs, slightly above that of conventional routes ($1,021 per ton)51, 52. In contrast, PET waste and PET textile waste yield substantially lower MSPs of $770 and $470 per ton, respectively. Overall, the hydrolysis recycling process represents an economically viable, environmentally sustainable technology for polyester waste disposal.
paper_content.methods:
Materials synthesis
Synthesis of pristine ZnO (p–ZnO). 0.01 M ZnCl2 (200 mL) solution was mixed with 100 mL deionized water. Next, 0.02 M NaOH (200 mL) solution was drop adding to form white flocculent precipitates under stirring for 1 h. The product was then harvested by centrifugation, washed several times with ethanol and water, and dried in a vacuum oven.

Synthesis of defect–rich ZnO (d–ZnO). 0.01 M ZnCl2 (200 mL) solution was mixed with 100 mL deionized water. Next, 0.02 M NaOH (200 mL) solution was drop adding to form white flocculent precipitates under stirring. After another 5 min, 0.01 M -ascorbic acid (200 mL) solution was added drop to the above solution, and the solution was stirred for another 1 h. The product was then harvested by centrifugation, washed several times with ethanol and water, and dried in a vacuum oven.

Catalytic performance of PET hydrolysis
PET hydrolysis was performed in a 20 mL reactor. 1.0 g of PET particles, 8 mL H2O, and the appropriate catalyst were added to a 20 mL high-temperature and high-pressure reactor under a stirring speed of 300 rpm. The mass fraction of PET and catalyst was 0.2%–2%. Then the hydrothermal reactor was heated to 190 °C for 6 h. Afterward, the reactor was cooled down to room temperature, and the products were separated from the solution by filtration to obtain terephthalic acid (TPA), without further purification. The purity of recycled TPA was according to national standard GB/T 30921.1. Conversion, yield, and space-time yield (STY) data were calculated by Eq. (1) (2) (3).

Conversion = (m(PET input)−m(PET residue)) / m(PET input) ×100% (1)

Selectivity = n(product i) / ∑n(product) ×100% (2)

Yield = n(TPA) / theoretical n(TPA) ×100% (3)

STY = m(TPA) / (m(cat)×t) (4)

Characterization
XRD patterns were recorded on a Rigaku D/MAX-2500 diffractometer using a filtered Cu-Kα radiation source (λ = 1.54056 Å). High-angle angular dark field-scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images were acquired by a JEM-ARM200F transmission electron microscope operated at 200 kV and equipped with a probe spherical aberration corrector. The XAFS spectra at Zn K-edge were acquired at the 4B9A station of the Beijing Synchrotron Radiation Facility (BSRF), operated at 2.5 GeV with a maximum current of 250 mA. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra were obtained on a JEOL JES-FA200. Low-temperature EPR spectroscopy measurements were conducted a spectrometer operating at the X-band frequency (EE500, Bruker). 1H-NMR spectra of TPA, Mode, and r-PET were collected by an AVI 400 MHz NMR spectrometer (Bruker). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of the samples were conducted using GeminiSEM 500.

In situ high-temperature and high-pressure infrared spectrometric experiments
To elucidate the depolymerization processes of Mode, in situ FTIR measurements were carried out using a Bruker Vextex 70 spectroscope equipped with a mercury-cadmium-telluride (MCT) detector. A background measurement was recorded to establish a baseline for subsequent measurements. Following this, H2O (10 L) was introduced into the reactor, the temperature was then incrementally increased from room temperature (~25 °C) to 190 °C at a controlled ramp rate of 10 °C min–1. Upon reaching 190 °C, this temperature was sustained for 60 minutes. Typical signals indicative of intermediates formed during the depolymerization processes were diligently captured and analyzed using FTIR spectroscopy.

Data availability
The data that supports the findings of the study are included in the main text and supplementary information files. Source data are provided with this paper. All data are available from the corresponding author upon request.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The paper is an interesting one - I would say that there are some aspects that need clarification before publication can be considered.
In the introduction the authors do need to make a more balanced argument about some of the catalysts that are available for the depolymerization of polyesters. There are some much better ones out there than the authors allude to.
During the mixed polymer recycling experiment why was the PLA not depolymerized - if the homopolymer was, would this not cause issues with a mixed feed? In the ESI table 5 needs more clarification - e.g. PLA/PET the yield of products in 100% but for PET/PE is is also 100% - the aspect of what is happening in the mixed polymer experiments needs more clarification/discussion.
The authors say this is scalable - but the largest experiment is 40g, whilst this is larger than most in the literature, I would not say this is scalable at this stage.
The mechanism section could be shorter - defects help and Zn acts as a Lewis acid are the more conclusions, which is what you might expect.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript describes the use of defect-rich ZnO (d–ZnO) nanosheets for the hydrolytic depolymerization of polyesters, including PET, under neutral aqueous conditions. The authors report high terephthalic acid (TPA) yields, good catalyst recyclability, and supportive mechanistic studies involving in situ spectroscopy and DFT calculations. While the technical execution is generally sound, this work suffers from a severe lack of originality and represents little more than a minor variation of the authors’ previously published research. Therefore, I do not recommend its publication in Nature Communications.
The central claim of this manuscript—that defect-engineered ZnO enables efficient polyester depolymerization—is not new. The same research group recently published a nearly identical study in Nature Communications (2024, 15:6266), where they reported defect-rich Fe/ZnO for methanolysis of PET. Both reactions proceed via nucleophilic substitution at the ester bond, and both rely on defect sites (oxygen/zinc vacancies) to activate the nucleophile—methanol in the prior work, water in this submission. The mechanistic narrative is essentially identical, merely adapted from methanol to water.
It is a routine extension of an established catalytic platform to a different solvent system. The scientific community does not need separate high-profile publications for every solvent variation of the same core chemistry, especially when the underlying principles and catalyst design are unchanged.
Other comments:
1. Many previously reported systems operate under milder temperatures or ambient pressure, whereas this process requires 190 °C and high-pressure water—conditions that are energy-intensive and industrially challenging. The claim of “mild conditions” is therefore disingenuous.
2. The current version of Figure 2 presents selectivity data for terephthalic acid (TPA), but yields are not clearly shown. Selectivity alone is insufficient to evaluate overall catalytic efficiency or to optimize reaction conditions, as it does not account for substrate conversion. For a meaningful comparison of catalytic activity across different catalysts or conditions, both conversion and yield must be reported. I recommend that the authors supplement Figure 2 (or its associated supplementary tables) with quantitative TPA yields to allow proper assessment of catalytic performance.
3. Given that the catalyst is a metal oxide operating under hydrothermal conditions, there is a non-negligible risk of Zn leaching, especially in the presence of carboxylic acid products such as TPA, which can act as chelating agents. reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript reports the development of a coordinatively unsaturated defect-rich zinc oxide (d-ZnO) catalyst that enables highly efficient, neutral-condition hydrolysis of diverse polyester wastes, achieving >99% yield of TPA with a STY significantly exceeding previously reported heterogeneous catalysts. Mechanistic studies suggest that defect sites promote activation of O2 and H2O, generating nucleophilic species that cleave ester C-O bonds. The process is further validated at tens-gram scale and shown via LCA and TEA to provide environmental and economic advantages over petroleum-based TPA synthesis and alternative chemical recycling routes. The work is generally novel, comprehensive, and impactful, and addresses a critical challenge in sustainable plastic circularity. The catalytic performance is impressive, and the mechanistic exploration is extensive. However, to meet the standards of Nature Communications, several issues require clarification or further experimental support:
1. The author should supplement the experiment with a blank control group without the catalyst to verify whether the catalyst has a catalytic effect.
2. The author fails to mention the recovery of ethylene glycol, another important monomer derived from PET hydrolysis, throughout the entire text. Ethylene glycol is also a crucial chemical raw material. Could the author elaborate on their considerations regarding the recovery of ethylene glycol?
3. Does the oxidation environment affect the chromaticity of the product TPA? Could the author provide a comparison of the chromaticity between the product TPA purified without activated carbon under optimal conditions and commercial TPA.
4. It is currently unclear whether O2 is consumed during the reaction process. By measuring the partial pressure of O2 before and after the reaction, it can be determined whether O2 functions as a co-reactant or a promoter.
5. Although recyclability has been verified in 5 runs, the leaching of Zn2+ was not confirmed through ICP-MS or XPS analysis, which is crucial for true heterogeneous catalysis.
6. The author should briefly comment on the potential environmental issues related to d-ZnO nanoparticles.

## Abstract

Closed-loop recycling of polyester waste offers a promising route for addressing the environmental burden of plastic pollution and enabling resource circularity. However, current polyester plastic recycling methods face limitations in industrial scalability and environmental impact. Here, we report the development of a low-cost, earth-abundant, coordinatively unsaturated defect–zinc oxide (d–ZnO) catalyst for the efficient depolymerization of various polyester wastes, including polyethylene terephthalate, biodegradable polyesters, post-consumer polyesters, and mixed polyester waste.

Mechanistic investigations reveal that defects structure in the catalyst enhance the activation of oxygen and water molecules, generating nucleophilic species that drive ester bond cleavage via carbonyl activation. The robustness and scalability of our strategy were further validated through large-scale closed-loop recycling of polyester waste plastics. Life cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analysis (TEA) demonstrate the environmental sustainability and economic viability of this process across multiple metrics, including human health, ecosystem quality, resource consumption, and production cost. This work offers a broadly applicable, sustainable, and practical solution for management polyester plastic waste.

---

## Introduction

Polyesters are synthetic polymers featuring ester linkages and are produced at a scale exceeding 70 million tons per year for use in packaging, bottles, and textiles1, 2. The widespread accumulation of polyester plastic waste has had profound impacts on the environment, marine ecosystems, and human health3–5. Chemical depolymerization of polyesters into monomeric constituents via hydrolysis6–9, alcoholysis10–16, aminolysis17, 18 and hydrogenolysis19–21 has been widely investigated. These processes offer a viable and scalable alternative to conventional end-of-life treatments, including mechanical recycling, incineration and landfilling22–25. However, pyrolysis and hydrogenolysis typically yield complex mixtures with low product selectivity. In contrast, solvent-assisted depolymerization of polyesters enables controlled cleavage of ester bonds to selectively yield targeted monomers. For instance, polyethylene terephthalate (PET) waste can be hydrolyzed in neutral aqueous media to produce terephthalic acid (TPA), which is suitable for repolymerization into recycled PET.

Nevertheless, conventional hydrolysis of polyesters typically requires harsh conditions, including strongly acidic or basic media or high-pressure systems (Figure 1a), leading to reactor corrosion, complex wastewater treatment, and elevated energy demands26, 27. Recent emerging strategies (including in situ alkaline hydrolysis, solvent-assisted hydrolysis, binuclear Zn-catalyzed hydrolysis, and acetic acid-mediated depolymerization) have improved PET conversion efficiency (Figure 1b)28–32. However, these methods often involve alkaline environments that necessitate post-neutralization and the use of mixed solvents, which complicate product separation and increase process energy intensity. Therefore, there remains a critical need for catalytic systems that enable selective polyester depolymerization under neutral, organic solvent-free conditions.

Homogeneous catalysts, such as ionic liquids and metal salts have demonstrated high activity in polyester depolymerization33–35. Recently, metal-based heterogeneous catalysts supported by auxiliary ligands have also been reported. For example, Dove and co-workers developed a highly stable bimetallic “acid salt” catalyst system capable of depolymerizing PET and polylactic acid (PLA), achieving activities up to 1.32×105 g mol –1 h–1 at 180 °C 36. In addition, Wang et al. reported a tetranuclear titanium catalyst that exhibits exceptionally high activity for PET methanolysis, reaching 1.9 ×107 g mol –1 h–1 at a catalyst loading of only 0.005 mol% 37. However, ionic liquids require tedious purification, and residual metal ions from metal salts catalysts can hinder repolymerization. In contrast, heterogeneous catalysts offer superior stability and ease of separation, making them attractive for polyester recycling.

Nevertheless, several key challenges persist: (I) limited interfacial contact due to poor multiphase mass transfer among solid polyester, water, and catalyst. (II) Polyester hydrolysis relies on activation of water molecules by catalytic sites to facilitate ester bond cleavage, underscoring the importance of enhancing the affinity and activation of water on catalyst surfaces. (III) Conventional approaches to improve heterogeneous catalyst activity focus on modifying particle size, coupling with ionic liquids, or employing porous materials. These mainly tune surface-active sites or increase external surface area, but can compromise catalyst–substrate mass transfer efficiency and reduce overall reactivity. To address these limitations, innovative catalyst designs and deeper mechanistic insights are essential for enabling efficient and green chemical recycling of PET waste.

In this work, we development of coordinatively unsaturated defect–zinc oxide (d–ZnO) nanosheets as an efficient heterogeneous catalyst for polyester hydrolysis (Figure 1c). Under neutral aqueous conditions at 190 °C, d–ZnO enabled complete depolymerization of PET, affording terephthalic acid (TPA) in >99% selectivity and achieving a space–time yield (STY) an order of magnitude higher than prior reports. The presence of oxygen molecules (O2) was found to be essential for enhancing catalytic activity, while the combination of defects in d–ZnO played a pivotal role in selective C–O bond cleavage. In situ infrared spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that defect sites facilitate the activation of water and O2 to generate nucleophilic species, which selectively attack ester carbonyl groups and promote bond scission. The catalyst demonstrated remarkable tolerance to additives and impurities across a wide range of polyester feedstocks. Moreover, we demonstrate the successful repolymerization of recovered TPA into recycled PET, enabling a closed-loop recycling process. Life cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analysis (TEA) comparisons against glycolysis, methanolysis, hydrolysis, and petroleum-based production systems confirm that this neutral hydrolysis approach offers superior environmental and economic performance. This work presents a viable and scalable approach for advancing circularity in polyester recycling.

---

## Results

Characterization of catalysts
To enable catalytic polyester depolymerization, we synthesized coordinatively unsaturated defect–zinc oxide (d–ZnO) nanosheets via an -ascorbic acid-assisted etching strategy. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images demonstrate that the d–ZnO retain the overall morphology and grain size of the pristine ZnO (p–ZnO) nanosheets (Figures 2a, b). Upon addition of -ascorbic acid, the sample color gradually changed from white to light yellow (insets of Figures 2a, b), suggesting structural changes. The strong interaction between -ascorbic and ZnO during the etching process promotes the generation of lattice defects. Although the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of d–ZnO and p–ZnO exhibit similar overall features (Supplementary Figure 1), noticeable changes in the intensity of the (002) and (110) reflections suggest the introduction of a significant number of lattices vacancies38.

Aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-STEM) revealed locally disordered lattice regions within d–ZnO nanosheets, consistent with the presence of unsaturated Zn coordination sites (Figure 2c)39. Zn K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra show a shift to lower energy for d–ZnO compared to Zn foil and ZnO, indicative of a lower oxidation state of Zn in the defective lattice (Figure 2d)40. Moreover, Fourier-transformed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (FT-EXAFS) analysis confirmed that the local coordination environment around Zn atoms in d–ZnO remains close to that of Zn–O bonding (Figure 2e). Electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy was employed to assess unpaired electrons associated with defect sites (Figure 2f). The signal at g = 2.002 is assigned to electron trapping by oxygen vacancies (Ov), while the signal at g = 1.950 corresponds to electron trapping by zinc vacancies (Znv)39, 41. Compared to p–ZnO, d–ZnO displayed substantially enhanced Ov and Znv signals, corroborating the L-ascorbic acid-induced formation of surface lattice defects.

Catalytic depolymerization of PET and real polyester waste over d–ZnO.
To investigate the catalytic depolymerization of polyester, polyethylene terephthalate (PET; number-average molecular weight (Mn) = 32 kDa, Supplementary Figure 2) was used as the model substrate. PET was reacted with the catalyst and water in a high-temperature and high-pressure reactor at 190 °C for 6 h. After cooling to room temperature, the products were collected and analyzed by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and gel permeation chromatography (GPC) to determine composition and purity.

We found that the reaction atmosphere plays a crucial role in determining product selectivity. Depolymerization reactions were conducted under nitrogen and varying concentrations of O2/N2 atmospheres using PET (Mn =32 kDa) as the substrate. Under a nitrogen atmosphere at 190 °C and neutral pH, p–ZnO exhibited minimal catalytic activity, yielding <5% PET conversion after 6 h. The product distribution included only 0.7% terephthalic acid (TPA), 4.3% oligomers (Figure 3a, Supplementary Figure 4, and Supplementary Table 1). Upon increasing the oxygen concentration from 1% to 10%, a marked decrease in byproduct formation was observed alongside a corresponding improvement in TPA selectivity, indicating the critical role of molecular oxygen in governing product distribution. At a 20%O2/80% N2 or under ambient air, complete PET depolymerization was achieved within 6 h, affording a TPA yield of 99%, and <1% yield of oligomers (Figure 3a, Supplementary Figures 5–12, and Supplementary Table 1). These findings unequivocally demonstrate that molecular oxygen is indispensable for promoting the selective hydrolysis of PET over p–ZnO.

To further optimize the reaction, the effects of temperature, reaction time, and catalyst dosage were systematically investigated (Supplementary Table 2), achieving >99% TPA yield with 99% purity under optimal conditions. The d–ZnO achieved substantially higher PET conversion and TPA selectivity compared to the p–ZnO and commercial ZnO (Figure 3b, Supplementary Figures 13, 14, and Supplementary Table 1), emphasizing the critical role of defect sites functionality in catalytic performance. Moreover, a series of defect–rich metal oxides were synthesized using analogous synthetic protocols. Their catalytic activities exhibited a strong correlation with the intrinsic Lewis acidity of the constituent metal ions, following the trend: d–ZnO > MgO > CaO > Co3O4 > MnO > Fe2O3 > Fe3O4 > Al2O3 >TiO2 > ZrO2 > Nb2O5 > CeO2 > SiO2 (Figure 3c, Supplementary Figures 15–38, and Supplementary Table 3), which closely aligns with the relative Lewis acid strengths of the corresponding divalent metal ions.

Under optimized conditions, PET waste was completely depolymerized over d–ZnO via hydrolysis at 190 °C within 6 h. The process afforded a space-time yield (STY) of 56 g h–1 g cat–1, which is an order of magnitude higher than those reported for conventional hydrolysis catalysts (Figure 3d, Supplementary Table 4). STY was calculated as the mass of product obtained per gram of catalyst per hour. Considering variations in previous reports, hydrolysis conditions were classified into four categories: (1) supercritical CO2, (2) acidic hydrolysis, (3) alkaline hydrolysis, (4) neutral hydrolysis, and (5) hydrogenolysis. Under neutral aqueous conditions (≥190 °C), d–ZnO exhibited significantly higher catalytic activity than previously reported systems. Even in comparison to supercritical CO2 and acidic or basic conditions, d–ZnO outperformed in catalytic efficiency. Notably, while acidic and alkaline systems can enable PET degradation at lower temperatures, they typically operate under harsh pH conditions (pH < 1 or pH > 10), raising environmental and operational concerns.

We further evaluated the depolymerization performance of d–ZnO across a variety of polyester substrates and mixed plastic waste. Structurally analogous polyesters to PET, such as polybutylene terephthalate (PBT) and polytrimethylene terephthalate (PTET), were efficiently depolymerized into terephthalic acid (TPA) with yields exceeding 99%, while poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) has a yield of 86%. (Figure 3e, Supplementary Figures 39–41, and Supplementary Table 5). Polycarbonate (PC) similarly depolymerized to bisphenol A (BPA) with yields >99% (Figure 3e, Supplementary Figure 42, and Supplementary Table 5). Encouraged by these results, we further explored the depolymerization of bio-based polyesters. Polycaprolactone (PCL) was converted into 6-hydroxyhexanoic acid, polylactic acid (PLA) into lactic acid, poly(butylene adipate) (PBA) and poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) into 1,4-butanediol, all with yields above 96% (Figure 3e, Supplementary Figures 43–46, and Supplementary Table 5).

To assess the practical applicability of our catalytic system, we examined the depolymerization of post-consumer PET waste and complex plastic mixtures using d–ZnO. In model systems containing PET and common packaging plastics (PLA, PC, PE, PP, PS, and PVC), selective hydrolysis of PET proceeded efficiently, affording TPA in yields exceeding 98%, with negligible interference from mixed plastics (Figure 3f, Supplementary Table 5). Remarkably, a wide range of real-world PET waste, including transparent and colored bottles was fully depolymerized under identical conditions, affording TPA in yields exceeding 99% (Figure 3f, Supplementary Table 5). These findings indicate that typical additives such as plasticizers, stabilizers, and antioxidants do not compromise catalyst performance. Depolymerization of polyester textiles and blended cotton/fabrics, despite the presence of complex additives like dyes, adhesives, and UV stabilizers, also affording TPA in yields exceeding 98% (Figure 3f, Supplementary Table 5). While dye removal remains a challenge in aqueous systems, nearly complete decolorization was achieved through activated carbon adsorption, although the fate of dye-laden carbon requires further attention. Remarkably, d–ZnO retained high catalytic activity even for complex substrates such as carpets composed of synthetic/natural fiber blends and various additives, affording >90% yield of TPA under ambient air conditions (Figure 3f, Supplementary Table 5).

Importantly, d–ZnO also demonstrated excellent performance in laboratory large-scale depolymerization of PET flakes (40 g), yielding over 34.5 g of high purity (>99%, Supplementary Figure 47) recovered TPA, which was subsequently repolymerized into recycled PET (r-PET). The r-PET was analyzed by ¹H NMR spectroscopy (Supplementary Figure 48), where the emergence of PET backbone signals at δ = 4.8 ppm confirmed the formation of r-PET. GPC revealed that the Mn =26 kDa of r-PET (Supplementary Figure 49), only slightly lower than that of the PET feedstock (Mn =32 kDa). The catalyst displayed excellent stability and recyclability, maintaining high activity and selectivity over five consecutive cycles (Supplementary Figure 50). Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) analysis of the digested TPA product confirmed that no Zn2+ leaching occurred. Following regeneration (see Supplementary Methods), the catalytic performance of d–ZnO was fully restored. XRD and SEM analyses (Supplementary Figure 51) confirmed that the regenerated catalyst retained both the crystalline structure and morphology of the original material. These results collectively underscore the robustness and versatility of the d–ZnO catalyst in addressing diverse streams of polyester waste, offering a promising avenue for closed-loop chemical recycling under mild, scalable conditions.

Mechanistic studies for the depolymerization pathway
To elucidate the evolution of active sites on the catalyst surface in the presence of reactive gas atmospheres and water molecules, semi-in situ electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy was employed to monitor signal variations of d–ZnO under air at various reaction temperatures (Figure 4a). The ESR signals at g = 2.002 and g = 1.950 are assigned to oxygen vacancies (Ov) and zinc vacancies (Znv), respectively, arising from the low-coordination environment induced by defect formation. As the temperature increased under air, the signal intensities of both Ov and Znv gradually increased, indicating that oxygen facilitates defect generation within d–ZnO42, 43. In contrast, under a N2 atmosphere, the Znv signal remained unchanged (Figure 4b), suggesting that defect evolution is suppressed in the absence of oxygen. To further probe the nature of surface-adsorbed oxygen species, low-temperature electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy was conducted at 110 K (Figure 4c). d–ZnO exhibited a pronounced signal at g = 2.001, attributed to surface-bound O3– species, whereas commercial ZnO showed no detectable signal. Upon heating to 150 K, O3– species are known to dissociate into monoatomic O– species, indicating that the active oxygen species stabilized on d–ZnO are predominantly O– species44.

To elucidate the activation mechanism of the solvent (H2O) on the surface of d–ZnO, in situ attenuated total reflectance fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIRS) spectroscopy was performed by gradually increasing the temperature from 25 °C to 190 °C. The v(O–H) stretching signal observed in the 3500–3150 cm–1 region corresponding to hydroxyl groups. A red shift of the v(O–H) stretching mode, along with an enhanced signal near 3150 cm–1, suggests that defect sites on d–ZnO promote interfacial water adsorption and O–H bond activation (Figure 4d)45, 46. We further evaluated the energy barriers associated with O2 and H2O activation on bulk ZnO, d–ZnO with oxygen vacancies (d–ZnO–Ov), and d–ZnO with zinc vacancies (d–ZnO–ZnVC), focusing on the O2 → O2* and H2O + O2* → OOH* + OH* steps (Supplementary Data 1). The local defect structures of d–ZnO act as anchoring sites for both O2 and H2O molecules, forming the initial state (S1). Water molecules adsorbed at S1* are activated by O2 to generate an intermediate species S2*, which further transforms into a transition state (TS), eventually yielding nucleophilic species in the final state. Notably, the activation energy for TS formation on d–ZnO–Znv is as low as 0.055 eV (Figure 4e, Supplementary Figure 52, and Supplementary Table 6), compared to 0.89 eV for d–ZnO–Ov and 1.24 eV for bulk ZnO (Figure 4e, Supplementary Figures 53, 54, and Supplementary Tables 7, 8). These results highlight the superior activity of defect structures on d–ZnO in facilitating both O2 and H2O activation pathways, which is critical for ester bond cleavage in PET depolymerization. This mechanistic insight aligns well with the in situ FTIR observations, emphasizing the essential role of d–ZnO defects in catalytic O2 and H2O activation.

To elucidate the depolymerization mechanism of PET over the catalyst, synchrotron radiation in situ infrared (IR) spectroscopy was employed using a dimer model compound (Mode) to simulate polyester conversion to monomers (Figure 4f, Supplementary Figure 55). The evolution of characteristic vibrational modes during hydrolysis was monitored in real-time to reveal potential intermediates and reaction pathways. At the initial stage, characteristic IR bands for Mode in H2O include the ν(C=O) stretching at 1,727 cm–1, ν(C–O–H) at 1406 cm−1, ν(C–O–C) at 1,338 cm–1, ν(C–O) at 1,259 cm–1, and ν(C–OH) at 1,083 cm–1 47, 48. With the presence of the d–ZnO sites, the ν(C=O) and ν(C–O–H) presented a red shift from 1,727 cm−1 to 1,708 cm−1 and 1,406 cm−1 to 1,390 cm−1, respectively (Figure 4f). This suggests that the carbonyl group produces a bond-weakening effect when coordinated to zinc sites, thereby enhancing the electrophilicity of the Mode31, 49. Notably, the ν(O=C–O) band at 1126 cm⁻¹ gradually disappears, accompanied by the emergence of a ν(C–OH) band at 1083 cm⁻¹, indicating cleavage of O=C–O–CH3 and O=C–O–CH2 ester bonds and the formation of methanol or ethylene glycol. These observations indicate that the ester C–O bond in Mode is cleaved, and methanol and ethylene glycol units are released and linked to form TPA. Meanwhile, the terminal groups are capped by hydrogen atoms to yield methanol and ethylene glycol, confirming that C–O bond cleavage within ester groups is the key step during PECT hydrolysis.

Hydrolysis experiments using model compounds (dimethyl terephthalate (DMT), bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET), and Mode-d4) were performed to elucidate ester bond-cleavage pathways. 1H NMR analysis showed that DMT hydrolysis produced terephthalic acid (TPA), with characteristic aromatic (8.13 ppm) and carboxyl (13.4 ppm) signals, while the presence of an O–CH3 signal at 3.89 ppm indicates cleavage at the O=C–O–CH3 bond (Supplementary Figure 56a). BHET hydrolysis similarly yielded TPA, with methylene resonances at 4.32 and 3.72 ppm confirming cleavage at the O=C–O–CH2 linkage. For Mode-d4, both O=C–O–CH3 and O=C–O–CD2 bond cleavage pathways were observed. Infrared spectroscopy further confirmed TPA formation, with benzene ring vibrations at 1574 cm–1 and C=O stretching at 1688 cm–1 (Supplementary Figure 56b). Residual O–CH3 (1192 cm–1) and CH2–OH (1065 cm–1) vibrations indicate partially hydrolyzed intermediates.

To gain further mechanistic insight into the role of catalyst surface defects in polyester depolymerization, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were conducted using Mode as the model substrate (Supplementary Data 1). The activation and cleavage of the ester C–O bond was examined on bulk ZnO, d–ZnO with oxygen vacancies (d–ZnO–Ov), and d–ZnO with zinc vacancies (d–ZnO–Znv). During depolymerization, the adsorption of OOH* and OH* on d–ZnO–Ov surfaces facilitate their interaction with Mode to form the initial state (IS1*, ΔE = –0.94 eV) (Figure 4g, Supplementary Figure 57, and Supplementary Table 9). Synergistic interactions between surface defects and OOH* species promote cleavage of the ester linkage (O=C–O–CH2), resulting in an intermediate state (IS3*, ΔE = 0.18 eV). Further transformation via the transition state TS1 (ΔE = 0.38 eV) drives scission of the C–O bond (O=C–O–CH3), sequentially generating TPA, 1-(2-hydroxyethyl)-4-methyl terephthalate (HEMT), ethylene glycol and methanol. The corresponding activation energies for this step are 0.56 eV on bulk ZnO and 0.52 eV on the d–ZnO–Znv (Figure 4g, Supplementary Figures 58, 59, and Supplementary Tables 10, 11). Similarly, the ester bond in HEMT (O=C–O–CH3) is activated and cleaved in the presence of OOH* and OH*, producing TPA and methanol via TS2 (ΔE = 0.46 eV). The activation energy barriers for C–O bond scission in HEMT is 0.49 eV on bulk ZnO and 0.52 eV on d–ZnO–Znv.

Based on the above findings, a schematic representation of the hydrolysis pathway catalyzed by d–ZnO is illustrated in Supplementary Figure 60. Molecular oxygen and water are first adsorbed and subsequently activated on the surface of d–ZnO, generating reactive OOH* and OH*species. These species nucleophilic attack the carbonyl carbon of PET, while the carbonyl oxygen is simultaneously activated by the d–ZnO of Zn sites. This synergistic effect enhances the cleavage of C–O bonds, leading to the formation of oligomers. Through a series of subsequent steps, comprising O2 and H2O activation, further nucleophilic attacks, carbonyl activation, and C–O bond scission.

LCA and TEA for closed-loop recycling PET
Sustainability assessments are crucial for evaluating the environmental, social, and economic impacts of recycling processes. To assess the environmental impact of the staged polyester recycling process, a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) was conducted using a cutoff approach50. Activity data for the process were obtained by constructing a conceptual factory model using Aspen software (Supplementary Figure 61). The model begins with polyester waste as the input stage and concludes with the recovered recycled polyester (Supplementary Table 12). The conceptual factory’s annual processing capacity is set at 250,000 tons, based on polyester waste statistics. The modeling process for staged polyester waste recycling includes several phases (Supplementary Figure 62, Supplementary Tables 13–15): (1) collection, transportation, and pretreatment of polyester waste; (2) catalyst synthesis, polyester depolymerization, and product separation; (3) repolymerization, and (4) melt extrusion and pelletizing. To improve modeling accuracy, experimental, literature, and industry data were incorporated into the comprehensive simulation of the entire recycling process. Background data on chemicals and electricity production were sourced from the ecoinvent v3.7 database.

Using recycled polyester pellets as the endpoint for assessment, the environmental impact of polyester closed-loop recycling process was compared with that of petroleum-based synthetic processes, including human health, resource consumption, and ecosystem impact9. Notably, the process demonstrated favorable performance in two critical metrics: Global Warming Potential (GWP) and non-renewable energy use (NREU). In China, the GWP is 2.830 kg CO2-eq/kg and the NREU is 40.377 MJ/kg (Figure 5a, Supplementary Table 16), which are approximately 47.3% and 55.1% lower than the petroleum-based production route, respectively. In Europe, the GWP is 2.236 kg CO2-eq/kg and the NREU is 38.125 MJ/kg (Figure 5b, Supplementary Table 16), which are approximately 7.2% and 45.5% lower than the petroleum-based production route, respectively. The key factors contributing to these impacts were the consumption of energy (electricity and steam) and chemicals. The polyester closed-loop recycling process significantly reduced environmental impact, primarily due to its integrated energy application and high recycling efficiency (Figure 5c, Supplementary Tables 17–26). Furthermore, we evaluated the environmental impact of d–ZnO across the full recycling process (Supplementary Figure 63 and Supplementary Tables 27, 28). Terrestrial ecotoxicity and non-carcinogenic human toxicity accounted for approximately 20% and 5% of the total impact, respectively, whereas contributions from other categories were minimal. The d–ZnO catalyst remained structurally stable throughout the reaction, and no Zn2+ leaching was detected, indicating that dissolved zinc species are not introduced into the environment. Additionally, a comparison with methanolysis, hydrolysis, and petroleum-based production processes (Figures 5d, 5e) identified core comparison metrics: global warming potential, and non-renewable energy use. With the exception of wastewater generation, which was similar to the petroleum-based production process, the hydrolysis recycling process outperformed the alternatives in all other metrics.

Through techno-economic analysis, we compared the total capital investment and unit production costs of the staged polyester closed-loop recycling process with those of the petroleum-based synthetic process (Figure 5f, 5g). The minimum selling price (MSP) of TPA was assessed for different production routes based on PET feedstocks (Supplementary Tables 29–35). Using clean PET sources results in a relatively high MSP of $1,049 per ton due to higher feedstock costs, slightly above that of conventional routes ($1,021 per ton)51, 52. In contrast, PET waste and PET textile waste yield substantially lower MSPs of $770 and $470 per ton, respectively. Overall, the hydrolysis recycling process represents an economically viable, environmentally sustainable technology for polyester waste disposal.

## Methods

Materials synthesis
Synthesis of pristine ZnO (p–ZnO). 0.01 M ZnCl2 (200 mL) solution was mixed with 100 mL deionized water. Next, 0.02 M NaOH (200 mL) solution was drop adding to form white flocculent precipitates under stirring for 1 h. The product was then harvested by centrifugation, washed several times with ethanol and water, and dried in a vacuum oven.

Synthesis of defect–rich ZnO (d–ZnO). 0.01 M ZnCl2 (200 mL) solution was mixed with 100 mL deionized water. Next, 0.02 M NaOH (200 mL) solution was drop adding to form white flocculent precipitates under stirring. After another 5 min, 0.01 M -ascorbic acid (200 mL) solution was added drop to the above solution, and the solution was stirred for another 1 h. The product was then harvested by centrifugation, washed several times with ethanol and water, and dried in a vacuum oven.

Catalytic performance of PET hydrolysis
PET hydrolysis was performed in a 20 mL reactor. 1.0 g of PET particles, 8 mL H2O, and the appropriate catalyst were added to a 20 mL high-temperature and high-pressure reactor under a stirring speed of 300 rpm. The mass fraction of PET and catalyst was 0.2%–2%. Then the hydrothermal reactor was heated to 190 °C for 6 h. Afterward, the reactor was cooled down to room temperature, and the products were separated from the solution by filtration to obtain terephthalic acid (TPA), without further purification. The purity of recycled TPA was according to national standard GB/T 30921.1. Conversion, yield, and space-time yield (STY) data were calculated by Eq. (1) (2) (3).

Conversion = (m(PET input)−m(PET residue)) / m(PET input) ×100% (1)

Selectivity = n(product i) / ∑n(product) ×100% (2)

Yield = n(TPA) / theoretical n(TPA) ×100% (3)

STY = m(TPA) / (m(cat)×t) (4)

Characterization
XRD patterns were recorded on a Rigaku D/MAX-2500 diffractometer using a filtered Cu-Kα radiation source (λ = 1.54056 Å). High-angle angular dark field-scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images were acquired by a JEM-ARM200F transmission electron microscope operated at 200 kV and equipped with a probe spherical aberration corrector. The XAFS spectra at Zn K-edge were acquired at the 4B9A station of the Beijing Synchrotron Radiation Facility (BSRF), operated at 2.5 GeV with a maximum current of 250 mA. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra were obtained on a JEOL JES-FA200. Low-temperature EPR spectroscopy measurements were conducted a spectrometer operating at the X-band frequency (EE500, Bruker). 1H-NMR spectra of TPA, Mode, and r-PET were collected by an AVI 400 MHz NMR spectrometer (Bruker). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of the samples were conducted using GeminiSEM 500.

In situ high-temperature and high-pressure infrared spectrometric experiments
To elucidate the depolymerization processes of Mode, in situ FTIR measurements were carried out using a Bruker Vextex 70 spectroscope equipped with a mercury-cadmium-telluride (MCT) detector. A background measurement was recorded to establish a baseline for subsequent measurements. Following this, H2O (10 L) was introduced into the reactor, the temperature was then incrementally increased from room temperature (~25 °C) to 190 °C at a controlled ramp rate of 10 °C min–1. Upon reaching 190 °C, this temperature was sustained for 60 minutes. Typical signals indicative of intermediates formed during the depolymerization processes were diligently captured and analyzed using FTIR spectroscopy.

Data availability
The data that supports the findings of the study are included in the main text and supplementary information files. Source data are provided with this paper. All data are available from the corresponding author upon request.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript describes the use of defect-rich ZnO (d–ZnO) nanosheets for the hydrolytic depolymerization of polyesters, including PET, under neutral aqueous conditions. The authors report high terephthalic acid (TPA) yields, good catalyst recyclability, and supportive mechanistic studies involving in situ spectroscopy and DFT calculations. While the technical execution is generally sound, this work suffers from a severe lack of originality and represents little more than a minor variation of the authors’ previously published research. Therefore, I do not recommend its publication in Nature Communications.
The central claim of this manuscript—that defect-engineered ZnO enables efficient polyester depolymerization—is not new. The same research group recently published a nearly identical study in Nature Communications (2024, 15:6266), where they reported defect-rich Fe/ZnO for methanolysis of PET. Both reactions proceed via nucleophilic substitution at the ester bond, and both rely on defect sites (oxygen/zinc vacancies) to activate the nucleophile—methanol in the prior work, water in this submission. The mechanistic narrative is essentially identical, merely adapted from methanol to water.
It is a routine extension of an established catalytic platform to a different solvent system. The scientific community does not need separate high-profile publications for every solvent variation of the same core chemistry, especially when the underlying principles and catalyst design are unchanged.
Other comments:
1. Many previously reported systems operate under milder temperatures or ambient pressure, whereas this process requires 190 °C and high-pressure water—conditions that are energy-intensive and industrially challenging. The claim of “mild conditions” is therefore disingenuous.
2. The current version of Figure 2 presents selectivity data for terephthalic acid (TPA), but yields are not clearly shown. Selectivity alone is insufficient to evaluate overall catalytic efficiency or to optimize reaction conditions, as it does not account for substrate conversion. For a meaningful comparison of catalytic activity across different catalysts or conditions, both conversion and yield must be reported. I recommend that the authors supplement Figure 2 (or its associated supplementary tables) with quantitative TPA yields to allow proper assessment of catalytic performance.
3. Given that the catalyst is a metal oxide operating under hydrothermal conditions, there is a non-negligible risk of Zn leaching, especially in the presence of carboxylic acid products such as TPA, which can act as chelating agents. Even trace metal contamination can compromise the purity of recovered TPA and hinder its repolymerization into food-grade or high-performance r-PET. Therefore, I strongly recommend that the authors analyze the Zn content in the purified TPA product to assess product purity. This is critical for evaluating the practical viability of the process.
4. On lines 229–231, the signal at g = 2.001 is assigned to surface-bound O₃⁻ species, while the signal at g = 2.002 is attributed to oxygen vacancies (OVs). These signals are very close in g-value, raising concerns about spectral resolution and assignment reliability. Please clarify how the authors deconvoluted these overlapping signals and whether simulations or power-dependent EPR measurements were performed to distinguish paramagnetic species. Additional justification or control experiments (e.g., isotopic labeling with ¹⁷O₂) would strengthen this assignment.
5. The use of the dimer model compound ("Mode") assumes that its reactivity reflects that of PET. However, the structure appears to contain two distinct C–O–C linkages: –O–CH₂CH₂– (ethylene glycol unit) and –O–CH₃ (methyl ester end group). The disappearance of the ν(C–O–C) band at 1,338 cm⁻¹ is interpreted as cleavage of the C–O–CH₃ bond. However, without isotopic labeling or independent verification, it is ambiguous which ether linkage is being broken. If the methyl ester group is preferentially hydrolyzed over the glycolic linkage, this would suggest a bias in reactivity that may not reflect real PET chain scission. The authors should either justify the choice of this model compound more rigorously or consider using a more representative PET-like dimer (e.g., bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate).
6. The claim that the merging of the ν(C–OH) doublet at 1,083 cm⁻¹ indicates “activation of interfacial water” (line 268) is speculative. This interpretation should be supported by references demonstrating similar behavior in well-defined systems, or by control experiments with deuterated water (H/D exchange).
7. On line 19, the phrase “Closed-loop recycling of polyester wastes of polyester waste” contains a redundant repetition (“of polyester waste”) and should be corrected for clarity and grammatical accuracy.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript reports the development of a coordinatively unsaturated defect-rich zinc oxide (d-ZnO) catalyst that enables highly efficient, neutral-condition hydrolysis of diverse polyester wastes, achieving >99% yield of TPA with a STY significantly exceeding previously reported heterogeneous catalysts. Mechanistic studies suggest that defect sites promote activation of O2 and H2O, generating nucleophilic species that cleave ester C-O bonds. The process is further validated at tens-gram scale and shown via LCA and TEA to provide environmental and economic advantages over petroleum-based TPA synthesis and alternative chemical recycling routes. The work is generally novel, comprehensive, and impactful, and addresses a critical challenge in sustainable plastic circularity. The catalytic performance is impressive, and the mechanistic exploration is extensive. However, to meet the standards of Nature Communications, several issues require clarification or further experimental support:
1. The author should supplement the experiment with a blank control group without the catalyst to verify whether the catalyst has a catalytic effect.
2. The author fails to mention the recovery of ethylene glycol, another important monomer derived from PET hydrolysis, throughout the entire text. Ethylene glycol is also a crucial chemical raw material. Could the author elaborate on their considerations regarding the recovery of ethylene glycol?
3. Does the oxidation environment affect the chromaticity of the product TPA? Could the author provide a comparison of the chromaticity between the product TPA purified without activated carbon under optimal conditions and commercial TPA.
4. It is currently unclear whether O2 is consumed during the reaction process. By measuring the partial pressure of O2 before and after the reaction, it can be determined whether O2 functions as a co-reactant or a promoter.
5. Although recyclability has been verified in 5 runs, the leaching of Zn2+ was not confirmed through ICP-MS or XPS analysis, which is crucial for true heterogeneous catalysis.
6. The author should briefly comment on the potential environmental issues related to d-ZnO nanoparticles.
